findings.title: Package does not exist on npm: @openai/codex-darwin-arm64
findings.description: The dependency `@openai/codex-darwin-arm64` is declared in package.json / package-lock.json but has no entry on the public npm registry.
findings.why: This is the AI-hallucinated-package failure mode. ~20% of package names LLMs recommend don't exist. findings.fix: Remove `@openai/codex-darwin-arm64` from package.json and any imports. Verify what you meant to install — this name was likely fabricated by an AI assistant.

findings.title: Date.now() feeding a sessionid — predictable secret
findings.description: A non-cryptographic random source (Date.now()) is being used to produce sessionid. Predictable across processes and observable within minutes to a determined attacker.
findings.why: Math.random() and Date.now() are deterministic pseudo-random generators. An attacker who observes a few outputs — or knows roughly when a value was generated — can predict the next one. That is the difference between a secret and a value the attacker already knows. Every OTP/token/session tutorial uses one of these because they 'just work' at demo time.
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() / crypto.randomInt() (Node) or crypto.getRandomValues() (browser). For OTPs: crypto.randomInt(100000, 1000000). For tokens: crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url').

findings.title: Wildcard CORS on an app with authentication
findings.description: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * lets any web page in a browser call this API. On an app with logged-in users this is catastrophic — combined with cookie or Authorization-header handling it enables full session hijack from any origin.
findings.why: This app has authentication (jose (JWT)). Wildcard CORS on an authenticated app means every credentialed request the browser sends can be triggered by an attacker's page. Every CORS tutorial writes '*' because that's the shortest snippet that makes an example work; the AI copied that.
findings.fix: Restrict origin to an explicit allowlist of trusted domains. Never combine `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials.

findings.title: Path traversal
findings.description: File read with user-controlled path may allow path traversal.
findings.why: A path like `../../etc/passwd` walks out of the intended directory. If any user input reaches a file read without allowlist checking, arbitrary file disclosure follows.
findings.fix: Validate paths against an allowlist. Use path.resolve and check prefix.

findings.title: Use of eval()
findings.description: eval() executes arbitrary code and is a security risk.
findings.why: eval() turns any user-controlled string into executable code. If any input reaches it, remote code execution is one line away.
findings.snippet: "Scan SKILL.md or README content from a GitHub repo for blocked patterns including eval(base64), " +
findings.fix: Remove eval() and use safer alternatives.

findings.title: Path traversal
findings.description: File read with user-controlled path may allow path traversal.
findings.why: A path like `../../etc/passwd` walks out of the intended directory. If any user input reaches a file read without allowlist checking, arbitrary file disclosure follows.
findings.fix: Validate paths against an allowlist. Use path.resolve and check prefix.

findings.title: SSRF (user-controlled fetch)
findings.description: Fetching a user-supplied URL may allow SSRF attacks.
findings.why: A server-side fetch on a user URL can hit the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) and leak IAM credentials, or reach internal services no external attacker could touch.
findings.fix: Validate URLs against an allowlist. Block internal IP ranges.

findings.title: Sensitive data logged to console
findings.description: Logging sensitive fields can expose secrets in log files.
findings.why: Log aggregators (Datadog, Vercel, Sentry, Papertrail) ingest console output. A password or token logged once ends up in log storage for the retention window — often 30-90 days.
findings.fix: Remove logging of sensitive fields or redact them.

findings.why: Log aggregators (Datadog, Vercel, Sentry, Papertrail) ingest console output. A password or token logged once ends up in log storage for the retention window — often 30-90 days.
findings.fix: Remove logging of sensitive fields or redact them.

findings.title: Math.random() used for security-sensitive value
findings.description: Math.random() appears to be used for non-security tracking, UI, correlation, delay, animation, or logging identifiers.
findings.why: Math.random() is a predictable pseudo-random generator seeded from clock/context. An attacker who sees a few outputs can predict the next one — fine for animation, catastrophic for tokens or OTPs.
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() or crypto.getRandomValues() instead.

findings.title: Math.random() feeding a apikey — predictable secret
findings.description: A non-cryptographic random source (Math.random()) is being used to produce apikey. Predictable across processes and observable within minutes to a determined attacker. Found in test file — likely intentional test fixture. Verify this is not a real credential.
findings.why: Math.random() and Date.now() are deterministic pseudo-random generators. An attacker who observes a few outputs — or knows roughly when a value was generated — can predict the next one. That is the difference between a secret and a value the attacker already knows. Every OTP/token/session tutorial uses one of these because they 'just work' at demo time.
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() / crypto.randomInt() (Node) or crypto.getRandomValues() (browser). For OTPs: crypto.randomInt(100000, 1000000). For tokens: crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url').

findings.title: Math.random() used for security-sensitive value
findings.description: Math.random() appears to be used for non-security tracking, UI, correlation, delay, animation, or logging identifiers. Found in test file — likely intentional test fixture. Verify this is not a real credential.
findings.why: Math.random() is a predictable pseudo-random generator seeded from clock/context. An attacker who sees a few outputs can predict the next one — fine for animation, catastrophic for tokens or OTPs.
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() or crypto.getRandomValues() instead.

findings.title: Date.now() feeding a apikey — predictable secret
findings.description: A non-cryptographic random source (Date.now()) is being used to produce apikey. Predictable across processes and observable within minutes to a determined attacker. Found in test file — likely intentional test fixture. Verify this is not a real credential.
findings.why: Math.random() and Date.now() are deterministic pseudo-random generators. An attacker who observes a few outputs — or knows roughly when a value was generated — can predict the next one. That is the difference between a secret and a value the attacker already knows. Every OTP/token/session tutorial uses one of these because they 'just work' at demo time.
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() / crypto.randomInt() (Node) or crypto.getRandomValues() (browser). For OTPs: crypto.randomInt(100000, 1000000). For tokens: crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url').

findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() or crypto.getRandomValues() instead.

findings.title: Date.now() feeding a sessionid — predictable secret
findings.description: A non-cryptographic random source (Date.now()) is being used to produce sessionid. Predictable across processes and observable within minutes to a determined attacker. Found in test file — likely intentional test fixture. Verify this is not a real credential.
findings.why: Math.random() and Date.now() are deterministic pseudo-random generators. An attacker who observes a few outputs — or knows roughly when a value was generated — can predict the next one. That is the difference between a secret and a value the attacker already knows. Every OTP/token/session tutorial uses one of these because they 'just work' at demo time.
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() / crypto.randomInt() (Node) or crypto.getRandomValues() (browser). For OTPs: crypto.randomInt(100000, 1000000). For tokens: crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url').

findings.why: Math.random() and Date.now() are deterministic pseudo-random generators. An attacker who observes a few outputs — or knows roughly when a value was generated — can predict the next one.
